question.text: A fair $12$-sided die with numbers $1$ through $12$ is rolled $20$ times. What is the probability that we get a number greater than $10$ more than $2$ times? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times that a number greater than $10$ is rolled.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=20$ rolls

  • the probability of getting a number greater than $10$ on any roll of the $12$-sided die is \[ p=\dfrac{2}{12}= \dfrac{1}{6} \]

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B\left(20,\dfrac16\right).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

\[ P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \]

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

\[ \begin{align*} P(X=x) &= \binom{20}{x} \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^x \left( 1-\dfrac{1}{6} \right)^{20-x} \\[5pt] &= \binom{20}{x} \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^x \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^{20-x}. \end{align*} \]

We want to find the probability of getting a "success" (i.e., a number greater than $10$) on more than $2$ rolls. This corresponds to $P(X > 2).$

However, computing

\[ P(X > 2) = P(X=3) + P(X=4) + \ldots + P(X=20) \]

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

\[\begin{align*} P(X > 2) &= 1 - P(X \leq 2) \\[5pt] &= 1 - \left[ P(X=0) + P(X=1) + P(X=2) \right] \\[5pt] &= 1 - \left[ \binom{20}{0} \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^0 \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^{20-0} + \binom{20}{1} \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^1 \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^{20-1}+ \binom{20}{2} \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^2 \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^{20-2} \right] \\[5pt] &= 1 - \left[ \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^{20} + 20 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right) \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^{19}+ 190 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^2 \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^{18} \right] \\[5pt] &= 1 - 0.328 \, 659 \\[5pt] &= 0.671 \end{align*}\]

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.text: The probability that John succeeds in selling an insurance policy to a given customer is $0.45.$ On a given day, he interacts with $8$ customers. Assuming that the transactions with customers are independent, what is the probability that he will sell at least $6$ insurance policies on this day? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of insurance policies that John sells on this day.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=8$ customers

  • the probability that John succeeds in selling an insurance policy to a given customer is $p=0.45$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(8,0.45).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

\[ P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \]

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

\[ \begin{align*} P(X=x) &= \binom{8}{x} \left(0.45 \right)^x \left( 1-0.45 \right)^{8-x} \\[5pt] &= \binom{8}{x} \left(0.45 \right)^x \left( 0.55 \right)^{8-x}. \end{align*} \]

We want to find the probability that John will sell at least $6$ insurance policies on this day. So, we compute

\[ \begin{align*} P(X \geq 6) &= P(X=6) + P(X=7) + P(X=8) \\[5pt] &= \binom{8}{6} \left(0.45 \right)^6 \left( 0.55 \right)^{8-6} + \binom{8}{7} \left(0.45 \right)^7 \left( 0.55 \right)^{8-7}+ \binom{8}{8} \left(0.45 \right)^8 \left( 0.55 \right)^{8-8} \\[5pt] &= 28\left(0.45 \right)^6 \left( 0.55 \right)^{2} +8\left(0.45 \right)^7 \left( 0.55 \right)^{1}+ 1 \left(0.45 \right)^8 \left( 0.55 \right)^{0} \\[5pt] &\approx 0.088 \end{align*} \]

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.text: A fair six-sided die is rolled $6$ times. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability of getting a $6$ exactly three times?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times that a $6$ is rolled.

Here, we have the following information:

  • There are $n = 6$ rolls.

  • The probability of getting a $6$ on any roll of the die is \[ p = \dfrac{1}{6}. \]

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X \sim B\left(6, \dfrac{1}{6}\right).$ We want to find the probability of $x = 3$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function \[ P(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1 - p)^{n - x}, \]

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get \begin{align*} P(X = 3) &= \binom{6}{3} \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^3 \left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^{6 - 3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6!}{3!(6 - 3)!} \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^3 \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^{3} \\[5pt] &= 20 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^3 \left( \dfrac{5}{6} \right)^3 \\[5pt] &\approx \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0.054}, \end{align*} rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.text: A new software program fails to run with probability $70\%.$ If it is tested on $5$ computers, rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that it fails on $1$ or fewer of them?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of failed runs.

Here, we have the following information:

  • There are $n = 5$ tests.

  • The probability of failure is $p = 70\% = 0.7.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X \sim B(5, 0.7).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function \[ P(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1 - p)^{n - x}, \] where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get \begin{align*} P(X=x) &= \binom{5}{x} (0.7)^x (1-0.7)^{5-x} \\[5pt] &= \binom{5}{x} (0.7)^x (0.3)^{5-x}. \end{align*}

We want to find the probability that $1$ or fewer of the $5$ software program runs fail. So, we compute \begin{align*} P(X \leq 1) &= P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) \\[5pt] &= \binom{5}{0}(0.7)^0(0.3)^5 + \binom{5}{1}(0.7)^1(0.3)^4 \\[5pt] &= 1(0.3)^5 + 5(0.7)(0.3)^4 \\[5pt] &\approx \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0.031}, \end{align*} rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.text: A soccer player has a $70\%$ chance of scoring a goal on a penalty kick. She takes $5$ penalty shots in a row. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that she scores at most $3$ goals?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of goals scored.

Here, we have the following information:

  • There are $n = 5$ penalty shots.

  • The probability of scoring is $p = 70\% = 0.7.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X \sim B(5, 0.7).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function \[ P(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1 - p)^{n - x}, \]

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get \begin{align*} P(X = x) &= \binom{5}{x} (0.7)^x (1 - 0.7)^{5 - x} \\[5pt] &= \binom{5}{x} (0.7)^x (0.3)^{5 - x}. \end{align*}

We want to find the probability that she scores at most $3$ goals. This corresponds to $P(X \leq 3).$

However, computing \[ P(X \leq 3) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + \ldots + P(X = 3), \] will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get \begin{align*} P(X \leq 3) &= 1 - P(X > 3) \\[5pt] &= 1 - \left[ P(X = 4) + P(X = 5) \right] \\[5pt] &= 1 - \left[ \binom{5}{4} (0.7)^4 (0.3)^{5-4} + \binom{5}{5} (0.7)^5 (0.3)^{5-5} \right] \\[5pt] &= 1 - \left[ 5 (0.7)^4 (0.3) + (0.7)^5 \right] \\[5pt] &= 1 - 0.528\,220 \\[5pt] &\approx \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0.472}, \end{align*} rounded to $3$ decimal places.
